newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Focus on June retail sales.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Focus on June retail sales.

text.p: The June retail sales report next Tuesday is likely to be the item of most interest to the U.S. credit markets in the coming week, analysts said.
On a calendar crowded with fresh economic news, the retail sales report will be "the main event," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo Mitsubishi.
"Retail sales has come to be known as our premier number for estimating how the economy is proceeding," Rupkey said. "So next week the focus will be on that."

Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that retail sales rose 0.2 percent in June after slipping 0.1 percent in May. Without auto transactions, sales are forecast at up 0.5 percent, after easing 0.1 percent in May.

"Consumer demand is key," said Rupkey. The reason is that if real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) picks up to "three percent plus" in the third quarter, the Fed will tighten at least once this year, he said.
"The FOMC minutes show that they're still tilted toward tightening," said Rupkey. "Certainly one tightening is in the cards if growth picks back up."
The Wednesday, the market gets the June Consumer Price Index (CPI), May business inventories, and June industrial production and capacity utilization data.

The CPI is expected to be up 0.2 percent, after rising 0.1 percent in May, according to economists polled by Reuters. The core CPI, the index without its more volatile food and energy items, is also expected to be up 0.2 percent, after rising 0.2 percent in May.
"We could see some inflation in the service sector," said David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston. "We might see some updrift reflecting higher hotel and airline rates."

A 0.3 percent rise in the CPI could upset the market, said Rupkey, noting that occasionally the market has rallied on a favorable wholesale price report (Producer Price Index) only to be dealt a setback by the subsequent CPI report.
But Rupkey and other analysts said the market is itching to go higher, a move that would push the benchmark 30-year bond yield below 6.50 percent.
The bond yield eased to 6.51 percent on Friday afternoon before selling trimmed the price advance and the yield backed up to close at 6.53 percent.

"Next week's economic calendar is terribly busy," said Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets. "Those who have not jumped on the bandwagon (as buyers) may find reasons to jump on next week."
Karydakis said the market is in "excellent" shape.
"It seems reasonably confident and solid and is just looking for a reason to go higher," he said.

The Philadelphia Federal Reserve's July survey of regional business conditions, due at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT on Thursday, might provide one of those reasons. Economists expect it to read 18, down from a reading of 25.3 in June.

"If the Philadelphia Fed survey confirmed the softness we saw in the June NAPM (National Association of Purchasing Mangement), that could lead people to believe that the economy in July is going to be soft," said Rupkey.
Other data that the market will have available to react to in the coming week include the June Atlanta Fed index on Monday, June housing starts due on Thursday and May U.S. trade data, due on Friday.
Dealers indicated that Federal funds would open at 5-1/2 percent on Monday.
